title: Single vs multi-agent: the decision
summary: Start with one agent. Add agents only when a named dial forces it: breadth that exceeds one context, tool overload, separate trust boundaries, or independent reads that can run in parallel.
useIf: Someone proposes a team of agents and you must decide whether the extra cost, latency and failure modes are justified.
avoidIf: Do not use a crew to fix a weak prompt, poor tools or missing evals, and do not parallelise coupled writes.

explain.md: The vendors who build agents agree on the default. Microsoft says to use the lowest level of complexity that reliably meets your requirements and calls a single agent with tools often the right default for enterprise use cases [[r9]]. OpenAI says to maximise a single agent's capabilities first, and to split when prompts hold many if-then-else branches or when tool selection fails after you clarify tool descriptions. Tool overload depends on similarity: some systems handle more than 15 distinct tools while others struggle with fewer than 10 overlapping ones [[r19]].

explain.caption: The six dials, one agent against many
head: Dial
Single agent
Multi-agent
Evidence
rows: Parallel reads cut time, handoffs and synthesis add hops
Parallel subagents cut research time by up to 90 percent, vendor-reported [[r2]]
Each worker gets a fresh window
Anthropic and LangChain list isolation as a benefit [[r6]][[r32]]
Separate security boundaries justify the cost [[r9]]

explain.md: The evidence is not contradictory. Anthropic's lead-plus-subagents system beat a single agent by 90.2 percent on its internal research eval, which is breadth-first reading. Cognition argued against parallel designs in 2025 and, on 2026-04-22, kept that view for parallel writers while reporting that agents contributing intelligence works when writes stay single-threaded and a clean-context reviewer checks the work [[r2]][[r3]][[r4]]. Both are vendor-reported.

pitfalls.symptom: The crew costs far more than the single agent and quality is about the same
pitfalls.cause: No baseline comparison on a golden set
pitfalls.fix: Measure the single-agent baseline first and keep the crew only if it wins on your eval.

pitfalls.symptom: Two agents produce contradicting pieces of one deliverable
pitfalls.cause: Parallel writers made implicit decisions without seeing each other's actions [[r3]]
pitfalls.fix: One writer, read-only helpers, and full traces shared instead of summaries.

pitfalls.symptom: Nobody can find where a run went wrong
pitfalls.cause: Failures hide in handoffs, verification gaps or misaligned goals [[r5]]
pitfalls.fix: Trace every hop, add an independent verifier and review traces with a MAST-style checklist.

scenarios.title: A tool list that keeps growing
scenarios.situation: A single agent has grown to dozens of tools from several teams. It picks the wrong tool about one request in five, and each team wants its own agent.
constraints: Many tools, several with overlapping purposes
Tool descriptions have not been reviewed
unknowns: Do overlapping tool names and descriptions explain the errors?
Can tools be loaded on demand instead of all at once?
scenarios.question: What do you do first?

options.name: Clarify and de-duplicate tool descriptions, load tools on demand, and split into specialists only if selection still fails
options.why: OpenAI's guidance is to split after clearer descriptions fail, and overlap is the usual cause of tool overload.
options.tradeoff: It takes careful tool review work, and the split may still be needed later.

options.name: Split immediately into one agent per team, behind a supervisor
options.why: It reduces tool lists per agent and gives each team ownership.
options.tradeoff: More hops and tokens, and the supervisor must still route correctly.

options.name: Raise the model's reasoning effort and keep every tool
options.why: More thinking does not fix ambiguous tool descriptions and it raises cost on every call.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable once descriptions are clean and errors persist on hard cases.

flips.then: Split by trust boundary regardless of tool count.

scenarios.takeaway: Fix the tools before you add agents.

scenarios.title: Separate data owners
scenarios.situation: Two teams own sensitive data in different systems with different permission models. One assistant must answer questions that touch both, and a prompt injection in one source must not reach the other.
unknowns: Does each system support delegated user identity?
How are results combined without leaking raw data?
scenarios.question: What do you build?

options.name: One agent per data owner with its own identity and tools, called by a supervisor that sees approved results only
options.why: Permissions stay with the owner and an injection in one source cannot reach the other tools.
options.tradeoff: More tokens, more hops and a combining step to maintain.

options.name: One agent with the union of both teams' permissions
options.why: A single injection could reach everything, and the blast radius is the whole union.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only when both systems sit under one owner and one trust boundary.

options.name: One agent using the user's delegated identity for both systems
options.why: Downstream systems enforce the user's rights, so access is bounded by the caller.
options.tradeoff: An injected instruction can still misuse the user's combined rights in one context.

flips.if: Rights are enforced only in the agent
flips.then: Do not rely on delegation, split the agents.

scenarios.takeaway: Trust boundaries can justify agents that parallel reads never would.

quiz.q: Which reading fits both Anthropic's research result and Cognition's argument?
options: Multi-agent always beats a single agent
Parallel reads across agents can pay off, but parallel writers to one artifact conflict
Both posts say never use more than two agents
quiz.explain: Anthropic's gain came from breadth-first reading with a lead and subagents. Cognition's concern was implicit conflicting decisions by parallel writers, and its 2026-04-22 follow-up kept single-threaded writes. [[r2]][[r4]]

quiz.q: Which dial changes justify splitting one agent into several?
options: Tool selection keeps failing after tool descriptions were clarified
The team wants more impressive diagrams
Different data owners need separate identities and permissions
The prompt has several if-then-else branches that a single prompt handles poorly
quiz.explain: OpenAI names branching prompts and failing tool selection as signals, and Microsoft names separate security boundaries. Diagram appeal is not a dial. [[r19]][[r9]]

quiz.q: A single agent run costs 40,000 tokens. Using Anthropic's reported multipliers, roughly how many tokens would a multi-agent run use if a typical chat is 10,000 tokens and multi-agent systems use about 15x chat?
quiz.hint: Apply 15x to the chat baseline, not to the agent run.
quiz.explain: The multipliers are relative to chat: 15 x 10,000 = 150,000 tokens. The agent run at 40,000 is about 4x chat, so the multi-agent run is roughly 3.75x the agent run. These are vendor-reported averages from one system. [[r2]]

flashcards.front: OpenAI's two signals to split a single agent?
flashcards.back: Prompts with many if-then-else branches, and tool selection that still fails after clearer tool descriptions. Tool overload depends on overlap [[r19]].
Parallel writers still fail. Multiple agents contributing intelligence works when writes stay single-threaded and a clean-context reviewer checks [[r4]].

flashcards.front: What is the token cost of each rung, per Anthropic?
flashcards.back: About 4x chat for an agent and about 15x for a multi-agent system, vendor-reported [[r2]].
